headline: Watakushi has no known source: a surface analysis suggests a compound, but no likely etyma are known.
Zōri: in late Middle Japanese the initial zo temporarily became an affricate, jo.
Futsū is Middle Chinese 普通, literally “ordinary + through”.
Chū is from Middle Chinese 註, and 注 is a daiyōji replacing 註.
Kuwashii is simply from Old Japanese.
Raishū is 来 (rai-, “coming..., next...”) plus 週 (shū, “week”).
Kokkai is from Chinese 國會 (guóhuì); the page also lists Korean 국회 (Gukhoe) and Vietnamese Quốc hội.
Haiiro is 灰 (hai, “ash”) plus 色 (-iro, “color”).
Inryoku is a calque of Dutch aantrekkingskracht, “attraction force”.
Hane is 羽 (ha, “feather”) plus 根 (ne, “root”), originally the spot where a quill meets the skin.
Otoshimono is 落とす (otosu) plus 物 (-mono).
Yunyū is an alteration of shunyū, using the kan'yōon yu for 輸.
Shoseki is from Middle Chinese 書籍 (MC syo dzjek).
Kaeri is the nominalized stem of 帰る (kaeru, “to return”).
I, “thoughts”, is from Middle Chinese 意.
Sōryō is 送 (sō) plus 料 (-ryō).
Dōitsu is from Chinese 同一, literally “same + one”.
Katagata is a reduplication of 方 (kata, “person”), with kata voiced to gata.
Hifu is a Sino-Japonic compound of Middle Chinese 皮 and 膚, first attested in 717.
Kuwaeru is from the Classical Japanese verb 加ふ (kufafu).
Saiwai is derived from sakiwai, and began as sakipapi.
Semeru, “to attack”, comes from the Classical Japanese verb せむ (semu).
Zettai was coined by Inoue Tetsujirō in 1881 as a calque of English absolute, changing the spelling from 絶待 to 絶対.
Tsuna is first attested in the Harima Fudoki of 715 CE, from Proto-Japonic *tuna.
Matsu might be a shift from 保つ (tamotsu, “to hold”), but the Heian accents do not match.
Bunkai is Middle Chinese 分解.
Zen is shortened from 禅那 (zenna), a Middle Chinese transliteration of Sanskrit dhyāna, “profound meditation”.
Nedan is 値 (ne, “price”) plus 段 (dan, “level”).
Fuku, “good fortune”, is from Middle Chinese 福.
Hōchō, a kitchen knife, comes from Middle Chinese 庖丁, “cook”.
